## Argument Definition
In TAPE, an argument is defined as a structured set of argument components within persuasive essays that aim to increase or decrease the acceptability of a controversial standpoint. Argumentative content consists of statements that function as a major claim, claim, or premise: the major claim represents the author’s overall standpoint, a claim is a central controversial statement within an individual argument, and premises are reasons that justify or refute a claim. Argument components are connected by directed argumentative relations of support or attack, where a source component provides a justification for or a refutation of a target component. An argument minimally includes a claim supported by at least one premise, and more complex arguments may include serial chains of premises. The paper explicitly distinguishes non-argumentative text as text units that do not contain argumentative content, such as introductory topic descriptions or other sentences without claims or premises.

## Annotation Guideline
Label a tweet/sentence as Argument if it contains at least one claim (explicit or implied), including major-claim-like stance statements; in multi-sentence tweets, the presence of any single claim makes the whole tweet Argument. Label No-Argument if required context is missing (e.g., it refers to an unavailable parent tweet) or if the text is not in English. Treat implicit claims (requests or prompts that presuppose a disputable point) as valid claims (e.g., “Show me the descriptions of skin colors in Tolkien’s writing” = Argument). Do not treat pure insults as claims; if the content is only insulting with no propositional assertion, label No-Argument (e.g., “don’t be a dick about it” = No-Argument). Argumentative content consists of statements that function as a major claim, claim, or premise: the major claim represents the author’s overall standpoint, a claim is a central controversial statement within an individual argument, and premises are reasons that justify or refute a claim. Argument components are connected by directed argumentative relations of support or attack, where a source component provides a justification for or a refutation of a target component. An argument minimally includes a claim supported by at least one premise, and more complex arguments may include serial chains of premises. The paper explicitly distinguishes non-argumentative text as text units that do not contain argumentative content, such as introductory topic descriptions or other sentences without claims or premises.

## Annotation Guideline
Label a tweet/sentence as Argument if it contains at least one claim (explicit or implied), including major-claim-like stance statements; in multi-sentence tweets, the presence of any single claim makes the whole tweet Argument. Label No-Argument if required context is missing (e.g., it refers to an unavailable parent tweet) or if the text is not in English. Treat implicit claims (requests or prompts that presuppose a disputable point) as valid claims (e.g., “Show me the descriptions of skin colors in Tolkien’s writing” = Argument). Do not treat pure insults as claims; if the content is only insulting with no propositional assertion, label No-Argument (e.g., “don’t be a dick about it” = No-Argument). Questions are generally non-argumentative unless they function as/contain a claim; rhetorical questions can introduce a topic but are not claims by themselves. Use cue phrases to spot argumentative content: conclusion/claim signals like “therefore/thus/as a result/consequently/so” and premise signals like “because/since/for example/in addition,” but do not rely on them blindly (they can mark intermediate steps). Argumentative content consists of statements that function as a major claim, claim, or premise: the major claim represents the author’s overall standpoint, a claim is a central controversial statement within an individual argument, and premises are reasons that justify or refute a claim. Argument components are connected by directed argumentative relations of support or attack, where a source component provides a justification for or a refutation of a target component. An argument minimally includes a claim supported by at least one premise, and more complex arguments may include serial chains of premises. The paper explicitly distinguishes non-argumentative text as text units that do not contain argumentative content, such as introductory topic descriptions or other sentences without claims or premises.

## Annotation Guideline
Label a tweet/sentence as Argument if it contains at least one claim (explicit or implied), including major-claim-like stance statements; in multi-sentence tweets, the presence of any single claim makes the whole tweet Argument. Label No-Argument if required context is missing (e.g., it refers to an unavailable parent tweet) or if the text is not in English. Treat implicit claims (requests or prompts that presuppose a disputable point) as valid claims (e.g., “Show me the descriptions of skin colors in Tolkien’s writing” = Argument). Do not treat pure insults as claims; if the content is only insulting with no propositional assertion, label No-Argument (e.g., “don’t be a dick about it” = No-Argument). Questions are generally non-argumentative unless they function as/contain a claim; rhetorical questions can introduce a topic but are not claims by themselves. Use cue phrases to spot argumentative content: conclusion/claim signals like “therefore/thus/as a result/consequently/so” and premise signals like “because/since/for example/in addition,” but do not rely on them blindly (they can mark intermediate steps). Claims are the ultimate goals of an argument and include policies advocated by a party or candidate, judgments about other candidates or parties, or stances and opinions toward controversial subjects that require justification to be accepted by the audience. Premises are assertions provided to support claims, functioning as reasons or justifications, and may take the form of past experience, statistics, examples, or other evidence. A sentence is considered argumentative if it contains at least one such argument component. Sentences that contain no claims or premises are treated as non-argumentative.

## Annotation Guideline
Label a tweet/sentence as Argument if it contains at least one claim (even implicit) that asserts a position, evaluation, policy, or judgment that could be supported or attacked; otherwise label No-Argument. Enforce dataset-specific exclusions: if necessary context is missing (e.g., refers to an unavailable parent tweet) or the text is not in English, label No-Argument. For multi-sentence tweets, any single claim makes the whole tweet Argument. Treat questions as Argument when they implicitly advance a claim or reasoning (e.g., “If Middle-earth is the whole ‘Earth,’ then why does the map extend…?”), and treat implicit prompts as claims when they clearly imply a stance/request for evidence (e.g., “Show me the descriptions of skin colors in Tolkien’s writing” → Argument). Do not count pure insults as claims (e.g., “don’t be a dick about it” → No-Argument). Use cue phrases as signals but not guarantees: claim indicators include “I believe,” “I think,” “in my judgment/opinion,” “I am in favor of,” “however,” “so,” “for this reason,” while premise indicators include “because,” “since,” and “for example”; still rely on context because indicators can appear without an actual claim. Boundary/nested case rule: a statement used as a reason may still be annotated as a claim if it is itself a disputable assertion needing justification (e.g., “Communism is the enemy of all religions” → claim/Argument even when functioning as support), and clauses are segmented by meaning (not punctuation), with no clause labeled as both claim and premise.

Claims are the ultimate goals of an argument and include policies advocated by a party or candidate, judgments about other candidates or parties, or stances and opinions toward controversial subjects that require justification to be accepted by the audience. Premises are assertions provided to support claims, functioning as reasons or justifications, and may take the form of past experience, statistics, examples, or other evidence. A sentence is considered argumentative if it contains at least one such argument component. Sentences that contain no claims or premises are treated as non-argumentative.

## Annotation Guideline
Label a tweet/sentence as Argument if it contains at least one claim (even implicit) that asserts a position, evaluation, policy, or judgment that could be supported or attacked; otherwise label No-Argument. Enforce dataset-specific exclusions: if necessary context is missing (e.g., refers to an unavailable parent tweet) or the text is not in English, label No-Argument. For multi-sentence tweets, any single claim makes the whole tweet Argument. Treat questions as Argument when they implicitly advance a claim or reasoning (e.g., “If Middle-earth is the whole ‘Earth,’ then why does the map extend…?”), and treat implicit prompts as claims when they clearly imply a stance/request for evidence (e.g., “Show me the descriptions of skin colors in Tolkien’s writing” → Argument). Do not count pure insults as claims (e.g., “don’t be a dick about it” → No-Argument). Use cue phrases as signals but not guarantees: claim indicators include “I believe,” “I think,” “in my judgment/opinion,” “I am in favor of,” “however,” “so,” “for this reason,” while premise indicators include “because,” “since,” and “for example”; still rely on context because indicators can appear without an actual claim. Boundary/nested case rule: a statement used as a reason may still be annotated as a claim if it is itself a disputable assertion needing justification (e.g., “Communism is the enemy of all religions” → claim/Argument even when functioning as support), and clauses are segmented by meaning (not punctuation), with no clause labeled as both claim and premise.

When the definition and guideline conflict, follow the guideline.
